Case Number:
25SMCV06536
Hearing Date:

March 12, 2026
Dept:

Background of
25SMCV06536
Kowal v. Sliver VR Technologies
On December 15, 2025, Jerry Kowal,
individually and derivatively on behalf of Sliver VR Technologies, Inc., filed
this action against Theta Labs, Inc. and Mitchell Liu as well as nominal
defendant Sliver VR. The complaint asserted causes of action for: 1. fraudulent
misrepresentation; 2. breach of contract; 3. breach of implied covenant of good
faith and fair dealing; 4. promissory estoppel; 5. retaliation in violation of
Labor Code §1102.5; 6. constructive wrongful termination in violation of public
policy; 7. unlawful, unfair, and fraudulent business practices in violation of
California Business & Professions Code § 17200 et seq.; 8. breach of
fiduciary duty (derivative); and 9. conversion (derivative).
On January 22, 2026, Judge Lisa K
Sepe-Wiesenfeld issued an order finding 25SMCV06536 and 25STCV36594 were not
related within the meaning of California Rules of Court, rule 3.300.
On February 9, 2026, Plaintiff filed the
First Amended Complaint adding causes of action for defamation, intentional
infliction of emotional distress, and negligent infliction of emotional
distress.

The FAC alleges Defendant Liu served as CEO
of both Defendant Sliver VR and its subsidiary, Defendant Theta Labs. Plaintiff’s
compensation included, in part, THETA tokens. The FAC alleges Liu had no
intention of creating a sustainable business, but rather utilized Plaintiff’s
connections to build public recognition and “pump and dump” THETA tokens. Plaintiff
further alleges Liu solicited employee investment, but refused to issue the
corresponding stock certificates as required. In 2021, Defendant Theta pivoted
away from the streaming and content delivery business and into the non-fungible
token (“NFT”) marketplace business. Liu allegedly directed employees to
generate false bids on NFT’s on its platform to manipulate the marketplace and
restricted employee allocations of Theta’s new cryptocurrencies while secretly
dumping Liu’s unrestricted allocations. The FAC further alleges anonymous
accounts on X (formerly Twitter) began posting defamatory allegations against
Plaintiff after he filed this action.
Background of 25STCV36594
Berry v.

Sliver VR Technologies
On December 15, 2025, Plaintiff Andrea Berry
sued Sliver VR Technologies, Theta Labs, Inc., and Mitchell Liu asserting
causes of action for: 1) whistleblower retaliation (Lab. Code § 1102.5); 2)
sex/gender discrimination in violation of FEHA (Cal. Gov. Code §§ 12926, 12940
and 12945); 3) failure to prevent discrimination and retaliation in violation
of FEHA (Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(k)); 4) fraudulent concealment; 5) wrongful
termination in violation of public policy;
and 6) willful failure to pay wages and waiting
time penalties Cal. Labor Code §§ 201, 203, 210, 218.
The complaint alleges Berry served as the
Head of Business Development and suffered retaliation for complaining about
illegal practices including consumer fraud, price manipulation and insider
trading, fraud against Theta’s business partners, theft, and/or infringement of
intellectual property, among other things.” (Berry Compl. ¶ 88.) The complaint
alleges Liu engaged in a “pump and dump” scheme for THETA tokens, engaged in
market manipulation on Theta’s NFT platform, obtained employee investments in POG
tokens through fraud, and failed to pay Berry half of the promised POG tokens
as part of Berry’s compensation.
This case is currently pending in Department 55
of the Stanley Mosk Courthouse.

Motion
On
February 18, 2026, Defendants
Sliver VR, Theta Labs, and Mitchell Liu filed the instant motion seeking to
relate 25SMCV06536 and 25STCV36594.
Opposition
In
opposition, Plaintiff Andrea Berry contends her choice of venue should not be
overridden and the cases are not related within the meaning of California Rules
of Court, rule 3.300.

Reply
In
reply, Defendants reiterate their argument that the cases should be related and
note an order relating cases does not impact Plaintiff’s choice of venue.
Motion
to Relate Cases
Standard
Pursuant
to Local Rule 3.3(f)(3), “[i]n the event that the judge designated under
California Rules of Court, rule 3.300(h)(1)(A)(B)(C) to make the decision, does
not order related any of the cases set forth in the Notice of Related Cases,
any party may file a motion to have the cases related. Department 1 shall hear
the motion, if the cases are all pending in the Central District or are pending
in two or more different districts.”
Department
1 Shall Relate the Two Cases
On January 22, 2026, Judge Lisa K
Sepe-Wiesenfeld issued an order finding 25SMCV06536 and 25STCV36594 were not
related within the meaning of California Rules of Court, rule 3.300. Accordingly,
the motion is properly brought in Department 1.
In opposition, Plaintiff contends her “choice
of venue is proper and should not be overridden” and the action was “properly
filed . . . in Los Angeles County Superior Court.” (Opp. at 2:18-3:9.) However,
an order relating cases does not affect venue, only courthouse and department
assignment. (
Glade v. Glade
(1995) 38 Cal.App.4th 1441, 1449 (“Even
though a superior court is divided into branches or departments, pursuant to
California Constitution, article VI, section 4, there is only one superior
court in a county and jurisdiction is therefore vested in that court, not in
any particular judge or department. Whether sitting separately or together, the
judges hold but one and the same court.”).)
Cases
are related when they (1) involve the same parties and are based on the same or
similar claims, (2) arise from the same or substantially identical
transactions, incidents, or events requiring the determination of the same or
substantially identical questions of law or fact, (3) involve claims against,
title to, possession of, or damages to the same property, or (4) are likely for
other reasons to require substantial duplication of judicial resources if heard
by different judges. (Cal. R. Ct., rule 3.300(a).)
Defendants
note the cases involve the same defendants and are based upon the same or
similar claims and contend “CRC 3.300 plainly does not require that all parties
must be identical. Indeed, cases have been related where the plaintiffs are
different” citing
Legal Aid Society of San Mateo County v. Department of
Finance
(2020) 59 Cal.App.5th 166, 179-180. (Mot. at 3:11-21.) However,
Legal
Aid Society
does not aid Defendants as the Court of Appeal merely noted “[t]he
two cases were ordered related pursuant to California Rules of Court, rule
3.300(h)(1).” (
Legal Aid Society of San Mateo County v. Department of
Finance
(2020) 59 Cal.App.5th 166, 180.) The Court of Appeal did not
address the propriety of relation or state which of the four grounds enumerated
in California Rules of Court, rule 3.300(a) applied. The cases do not involve
the same parties as each is brought by a different Plaintiff. (Cal. R. Ct.,
rule 3.300(a)(1).) The cases also do not involve property claims. (Cal. R. Ct.,
rule 3.300(a)(3).)
However,
as argued by Defendants, the cases do arise from substantially identical
incidents, or events requiring the determination of the same or substantially
identical questions of law or fact, (Cal. R. Ct., rule 3.300(a)(2)), and are
likely for other reasons to require a substantial duplication of judicial
resources if heard by different judges. (Cal. R. Ct., rule 3.300(a)(4).)
Plaintiff’s attempts in opposition to highlight differences in the two cases
does not render the cases unrelated.
In
both cases, Plaintiffs allege they relied upon Defendants’ representations and
omissions when purchasing POG tokens in support of their fraud claims. (Berry
Compl. ¶¶ 53-63, 118-121; Kowal FAC ¶¶ 123-130.) The Kowal FAC further contains
allegations regarding Liu’s communications with employees, such as Berry, regarding
investment into the POG tokens. (Kowal FAC ¶¶ 158, 183.) Plaintiffs’ complaints
both allege Liu engaged in market manipulation related to various
cryptocurrencies and NFTs, and misrepresented its AI Chatbot as being
proprietary software, when it was merely a ChatGPT product. (Berry Compl. ¶¶
32-35; Kowal FAC ¶¶ 86-88.) Both complaints also contain allegations regarding
an improper kickback scheme in connection with the Secret Pineapple Society
NFTs, (Berry Compl. ¶¶ 42-51; Kowal FAC ¶¶ 77-81), and Berry expressly alleges
she reported her concerns to Liu with Kowal. (Berry Compl. ¶ 45.) Both
Plaintiffs assert whistleblower retaliation claims based upon the same
perceived unlawful conduct. (Berry Compl. ¶ 88; Kowal FAC ¶¶ 158.) Having a
single judicial officer preside over the significant overlapping allegations
regarding Defendants’ conduct promotes judicial efficiency and reduces the
potential for conflicting orders, including on clearly overlapping discovery. (
Tritek
Telecom, Inc. v. Superior Court
(2009) 169 Cal.App.4th 1385, 1390 (“we note
that four separate but related matters were assigned to three different judges
and there is a possibility of conflicting rulings on discovery matters. There
are rules to prevent this.”).)
The
Court finds the cases are related within the meaning of California Rules of
Court, rule 3.300 and the motion is GRANTED.
Conclusion
Defendants’
Motion to Relate and Reassign Cases is GRANTED.
Department
1 relates 25SMCV06536 with 25STCV36594 and orders 25STCV36594 reassigned to
Department N of the Santa Monica Courthouse for all purposes. All hearings
currently set in 25STCV36594 are hereby advanced and vacated.
Counsel
for Moving Parties is ordered to give notice.
